exhibit.title: Bounded ping result
exhibit.text:
Sending 5, 100-byte ICMP Echos; timeout 2 seconds:
.!!!!
Success rate: 80 percent (4/5)

prompt: What does this ping result show?
options: The destination enforced a four-reply ICMP limit for this source.
One request did not receive a reply within its wait; the cause needs more evidence.
A routing update installed the route immediately after the first request.
The first request was definitely discarded during ARP resolution.
explanation: The period means one request timed out and each exclamation mark is an echo reply. The cause of the timeout needs more evidence.

whyWrong.0: Four replies do not show a configured reply limit.
whyWrong.2: The output shows no routing change.
whyWrong.3: The output contains no ARP information.

exhibit.title: Ping response characters
exhibit.text:
R1# ping 10.0.50.1
U.U.U
Success rate: 0 percent

prompt: What do the U characters in this ping mean?
options: Destination-unreachable responses were reported for some probes.
The source router had no usable interface for every probe.
The destination application accepted and then closed its connections.
Each period proves a fixed 500-ms ICMP response limiter on R2.
explanation: U means a destination-unreachable message came back for that probe, unlike a period, which is a timeout. Check the source of the ICMP message and its code.

whyWrong.1: U does not mean every interface on the source router was unusable.
whyWrong.2: A ping does not open an application connection.
whyWrong.3: A U is an unreachable message, not a rate limiter.

prompt: Which two statements correctly compare IOS traceroute and Windows tracert? Select two.
options: IOS normally uses ICMP echo while Windows normally uses UDP.
Windows tracert normally uses ICMP echo requests.
IOS normally uses UDP probes toward high destination ports.
Both tools must use the same probe transport to discover any hops.
explanation: Both tools increase the TTL one hop at a time and collect time-exceeded replies. IOS traceroute sends UDP probes to high ports and Windows tracert sends ICMP echo requests.

whyWrong.3: Both tools find hops with different probe types because each hop answers with time exceeded.

prompt: Which two statements about these tables are accurate? Select two.
options: An absent ARP entry proves the host has never received a neighbor reply.
A dynamic MAC entry identifies a VLAN/port that learned that source MAC.
An incomplete ARP entry shows resolution is incomplete at this observation.
A learned MAC establishes the host has the correct mask and gateway.
explanation: A dynamic MAC table entry shows which port and VLAN learned a source MAC. An incomplete ARP entry means no reply has arrived yet.

whyWrong.0: ARP entries age out or are cleared, so a missing entry does not show a reply was never received.
whyWrong.3: MAC learning says nothing about the host's mask or gateway.

exhibit.title: Routed Ethernet state
exhibit.text: Gi0/1 10.0.99.1 YES manual down down

prompt: What should you check first on this routed Ethernet interface?
options: Remove a local shutdown command, which this status explicitly proves.
Change the IP mask before checking whether either end has carrier.
Replace the cable immediately because down/down uniquely proves its failure.
Inspect local media and the connected peer's current link state.
explanation: Down/down means the physical layer is down. Check the local media and the peer's link state; a local `shutdown` appears as administratively down instead.

whyWrong.0: A local shutdown shows administratively down, not down/down.
whyWrong.1: A mask error does not affect carrier.
whyWrong.2: Down/down can come from a disabled or unpowered peer, so it does not prove a bad cable.

exhibit.title: Both-end duplex and current counters
exhibit.text:
SW1 Fa0/24: 100 Mb/s, half duplex; late collisions rose 40→65
R1 Gi0/0: speed 100; duplex full

prompt: Which problem should you fix first?
options: Late collisions establish damaged copper regardless of the peer settings.
The displayed half/full settings establish a duplex mismatch.
The rising late collisions measure output-queue congestion.
The two 100-Mb/s values establish a negotiated speed mismatch.
explanation: The exhibit shows half duplex on SW1 and full duplex on R1, which is a duplex mismatch. Set matching duplex on both ends.

whyWrong.0: Late collisions here result from the mismatch, not damaged copper.
whyWrong.2: Late collisions are not output-queue drops.
whyWrong.3: Both ends show 100 Mb/s, so the speeds match.

exhibit.title: Trace with a silent intermediate hop

prompt: A web application is slow. What does this traceroute show?
options: The destination replies certify that HTTP performance is normal.
The three stars establish three seconds of forwarding delay for each user packet.
The third router dropped every packet and caused the slow application.
Later probes received replies, so the middle stars alone do not prove a forwarding break.
explanation: A star means a probe got no reply within the wait, and later hops answered. Stars in the middle therefore do not show a forwarding break.

whyWrong.0: Traceroute does not test HTTP performance.
whyWrong.1: A timeout is not a measurement of forwarding delay.
whyWrong.2: Later hops replied, so traffic is not stopping at the third router.

exhibit.title: Logging threshold and two messages
exhibit.text:
logging trap warnings
%LINK-3-UPDOWN: Gi0/1 changed state to down
%LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Gi0/1 line protocol changed state to down

prompt: Which message does this threshold send to the remote syslog server?
options: Neither message is selected because warnings means exactly severity 4.
Only the severity-5 LINEPROTO message is selected by this threshold.
Both messages are selected because both concern the same interface.
Only the severity-3 LINK message is selected by this threshold.
explanation: A logging threshold includes the named level and all more severe (lower-numbered) levels. Warnings is severity 4, so the severity-3 message is sent.

whyWrong.0: The threshold includes severities 0 to 4, not only 4.
whyWrong.1: Severity 5 is less severe than the warnings threshold.
whyWrong.2: Each message is filtered by its own severity.

prompt: What does this client-side TCP capture show?
options: A matching reset was received; identify the generating endpoint or intermediary before attributing the refusal.
The reset proves the client cannot receive any packet from that direction.
The SYN was silently discarded and no response reached the client.
The capture alone proves the application server itself generated the reset.
explanation: A matching reset is an active reply, unlike a silent drop. A firewall can send resets too, so check the server side before blaming the server.

whyWrong.1: The reset itself arrived from that direction.
whyWrong.2: A matching RST is a response, not silence.
whyWrong.3: The source address of a reset does not prove the server sent it.

exhibit.title: Received ICMP error
exhibit.text:
10.0.99.2 → 10.0.10.50
ICMP Destination Unreachable: communication administratively prohibited (type 3, code 13)

prompt: What should you check next, given this received ICMP error?
options: Replace the missing default route that this code uniquely identifies.
Correct the expired TTL that is explicitly reported in this message.
Inspect administrative forwarding policy at the reporting device and the matching flow.
Repair ARP for the destination because this is a host-unreachable code.
explanation: Type 3 code 13 means communication is administratively prohibited. Look at the access policy on the reporting device.

whyWrong.0: A missing route gives a different unreachable code.
whyWrong.1: TTL expiry is a time-exceeded message, not this one.
whyWrong.3: Host unreachable is a different code.

prompt: Which IOS ping tests whether a 1500-byte IPv4 packet passes the path without fragmenting?
options: ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1 repeat 5 size 1500 df-bit
ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1 repeat 5 size 1472
ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1 repeat 5 size 100 df-bit
ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1 repeat 5 size 1500
explanation: `size 1500` sets the datagram size and `df-bit` forbids fragmentation, so a smaller path MTU produces an error or a timeout.

whyWrong.1: Size 1472 is not a 1500-byte datagram, and DF is not set.
whyWrong.2: A 100-byte packet does not test a large size.
whyWrong.3: Without DF, the router can fragment the packet.

exhibit.title: Two independent switch-port conditions
exhibit.text:
Fa0/3: err-disabled
Fa0/4: inactive, configured access VLAN 30
show vlan brief: VLAN 30 absent

prompt: The design requires VLAN 30 on Fa0/4, and Fa0/3 is err-disabled. Which pair of actions fits the evidence?
options: Move both ports to an existing VLAN without checking their intended subnets.
Replace both cables before inspecting the recorded state and VLAN database.
Inspect Fa0/3's protection cause and restore the intended VLAN 30 for Fa0/4.
Enable Fa0/3 without checking why its protection acted.
explanation: Find out why Fa0/3 was err-disabled before bringing it back up. The VLAN list shows VLAN 30 is missing, so create it for Fa0/4.

whyWrong.0: Moving ports to another VLAN changes the design and leaves VLAN 30 missing.
whyWrong.1: The evidence does not point to cable damage.
whyWrong.3: Re-enabling without finding the cause can trigger the same err-disable again.

prompt: What happened to CRC errors during the measured interval?
options: There were 900 new CRC errors during this transfer.
The retained total proves that the present cable must be replaced.
The 2,000,000 packets prove that no loss occurred elsewhere.
No new CRC errors were counted on this interface during the interval.
explanation: The CRC counter stayed at 900, so there were no new CRC errors during the test. The 900 is the retained total.

whyWrong.0: 900 is the retained total, not new errors.
whyWrong.1: An old total does not prove a present cable fault.
whyWrong.2: One interface's counter does not show loss elsewhere on the path.

exhibit.title: Counters bracketing one controlled transfer
exhibit.text:
Same interface; no counter clear or reboot.
Before: 1,000,000 input packets; 900 CRC
After: 3,000,000 input packets; 900 CRC

prompt: The TCP connection completes and the server returns an application error. Where should you investigate next?
options: Inspect the responding application and its dependencies for the reported failure.
Change the client resolver and repeat the same lookup before examining the service.
Add a host route to the approved server to repair the unsuccessful request.
Raise the TCP connection timeout and retry before checking the service response.
explanation: A completed connection and an application response show the network path works. Investigate the service and its dependencies.

whyWrong.1: The lookup already returned the approved address.
whyWrong.2: A complete TCP exchange does not need a new route.
whyWrong.3: The request got a response, so it did not time out.

exhibit.title: One captured application transaction
exhibit.text:
Intended name resolves to the approved IPv4 address.
TCP SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK complete for that address.
HTTP response to the request: 503 Service Unavailable.

prompt: Which evidence do you still need before closing the incident?
options: A repeat of R1's successful directly connected peer ping.
A screenshot showing the exact intended configuration line.
A fresh original-service test from the affected client.
An updated uptime display after restarting the router.
explanation: A router test and a route change do not prove the client's whole path works. Retest the original service from the affected client and record the result.

whyWrong.0: A router's own ping tests a narrower path.
whyWrong.1: A configuration line shows intent, not delivery.
whyWrong.3: A restart is not an acceptance test and can erase useful evidence.

exhibit.title: Repair acceptance record
exhibit.text:
Original complaint: PC-A cannot load the named application.
A missing route was restored.
R1 can ping the server.
No PC-A application test has been repeated.

exhibit.title: Same DHCP attempt at two capture points
exhibit.text:
Server-side: relayed Discover received; Offer sent to giaddr 10.0.10.1
Client-side: Discover transmitted; no Offer observed in the same interval

prompt: These captures come from the same DHCP attempt. What should you investigate?
options: Investigate delivery of the Offer from the server through the relay to the client.
The client certainly received the ACK but lost its default gateway setting.
The helper must be absent because no server reply can exist without it.
The server certainly had no matching pool and never constructed an Offer.
explanation: The server sent an Offer, but the client never saw it. Check the relay and the return path for the Offer.

whyWrong.1: No ACK was received.
whyWrong.2: The Discover was forwarded and a reply left the server, so the helper works.
whyWrong.3: The server did send an Offer, so its pool matched.

prompt: A DF-bit ping returns a fragmentation-needed error, and a smaller ping succeeds. Which follow-up fits?
options: Treat the error as evidence of a size constraint; inspect the reported MTU and a smaller DF probe.
Treat both tests as proof that the server is down at every packet size.
Replace DNS settings because a larger numeric-address probe cannot resolve the name.
Remove DF and call the original unfragmented-size requirement verified if a reply arrives.
explanation: A fragmentation-needed error reports an MTU limit on the path. Note the reporting device and its MTU, then retest with a smaller DF packet.

whyWrong.1: The smaller probe got replies, so the server is up.
whyWrong.2: The test already uses a numeric address, so DNS is not involved.
whyWrong.3: A reply after removing DF does not show the original unfragmented size passes.

exhibit.title: Controlled IPv4 size comparison
exhibit.text:
Same source and destination, ordinary 20-byte IPv4 header.
100-byte DF datagrams receive replies.
1500-byte DF datagrams receive ICMP fragmentation-needed errors.
No numeric next-hop MTU has yet been read.

prompt: Two devices' logs show events with different clock times. What should you do before ordering them?
options: R2 must have caused R1's event because its printed time is earlier.
Record each clock's uncertainty and correlate a shared observation before ordering the events.
Use the collector's arrival order as proof of the devices' event order.
Subtract the displayed times and report a measured propagation delay.
explanation: Device clocks that are not synchronized cannot order events across devices. Record each clock's offset or find a shared event first.

whyWrong.0: An earlier time on an unverified clock does not prove cause.
whyWrong.2: Arrival order at the collector depends on buffering and paths.
whyWrong.3: The difference includes unknown clock offset, so it is not propagation delay.

exhibit.title: Log times from two devices
exhibit.text:
R1: *10:15:01 link event; clock not authoritative
R2: 10:14:58 neighbor event; synchronization not checked
Collector receives R1's message first.

prompt: The route is fixed and the numeric-address service works, but the name still resolves wrongly. What is the next action?
options: Undo the route repair and return to investigating the original missing route.
Correct the stale DNS record, then test a fresh answer and the named application.
Clear only the client DNS cache and close the incident after a numeric-address test.
Assign the server the stale address .99 to avoid changing the DNS service.
explanation: The numeric service works and the DNS answer is still wrong, so the DNS record is a separate fault. Correct the record, then test a fresh answer and the named service.

whyWrong.0: The route fix worked, so the original route problem is solved.
whyWrong.2: The resolver itself returns the wrong answer, so a client cache clear does not fix it.
whyWrong.3: The server stays at .10, and renumbering it to match stale DNS changes the design.

exhibit.title: Checks after a routing repair
exhibit.text:
Approved server: 10.31.20.10.
PC-A HTTP to 10.31.20.10 now succeeds.
Fresh direct query to its intended resolver: app.lab.example A = 10.31.20.99.
The DNS configuration confirms that stale address; .99 is unused.

prompt: Which two conclusions does the evidence support? Choose two.
options: This interface has counted new outgoing drops during the interval.
The clean CRC count certifies every cable in the network.
Raising a buffer limit would guarantee recovery without any further evidence.
The switch must have a duplex mismatch despite both endpoints showing full.
The displayed queue evidence is relevant to local egress congestion.
explanation: New outgoing drops and a full egress queue indicate congestion on this interface's output. They do not show the source of the load or prove the rest of the path is clean.

whyWrong.1: A clean counter on one interface does not certify other cables.
whyWrong.2: A larger buffer does not guarantee recovery.
whyWrong.3: Both ends show full duplex, so there is no mismatch.

exhibit.title: Current egress observations
exhibit.text:
During one test: output drops 50→150.
Receive CRC unchanged at 0.
Both endpoints operate full duplex.
The egress queue reaches its configured limit during the test.

exhibit.title: Tests with different source addresses
exhibit.text:
R1 source 10.0.99.1 → 10.0.20.10: success
R1 source 10.0.10.1 → 10.0.20.10: failure
PC-A 10.0.10.50/24: local gateway ping succeeds

prompt: R1 can ping the server from its transit source but not from its LAN source. What should you check next?
options: Retest from the transit source and close the issue if it succeeds again.
Add another R1 route to the server subnet before checking the reply destination.
Inspect the server return routes and source-dependent policy for the LAN source.
Replace the PC access cable, then repeat only the router-source test.
explanation: The source address becomes the reply destination, so a different source can use a different return route or policy. Check the server's return route and any source-based policy for the LAN source.

whyWrong.0: A second pass from the transit source does not test the LAN source.
whyWrong.1: The forward route works for the transit source, so check the return path first.
whyWrong.3: A router-originated test does not use the PC's access cable.

prompt: An analyzer shows gaps in a TCP capture. Which measurement best tests whether packets were actually lost on the path?
options: Count the analyzer warnings and report that count as packets lost on the server link.
Run a short ping after the transfer and use its loss percentage as the TCP loss rate.
Capture a different successful flow and use that result to dismiss the original gaps.
Compare a complete capture at a second point for the same flow and interval.
explanation: Gaps in a capture can mean the capture itself missed packets. Compare a complete capture of the same flow at a second point.

whyWrong.0: Analyzer warnings count missing capture data, not packets lost on a link.
whyWrong.1: A later ping is not the same flow or time.
whyWrong.2: A different flow can be treated differently.

exhibit.title: Capture coverage and application evidence
exhibit.text:
Client transfer completes, but intermittently slowly.
Capture tool reports dropped capture packets.
Wireshark labels a gap: Previous segment not captured.
No second capture or current interface counter interval is available.

prompt: The request reaches the server but no reply returns. Which check best separates a wrong return next hop from a forward-path failure?
options: Install another R2 route to the client subnet before examining the server route.
Inspect the server's selected route and neighbor resolution for the client reply.
Ping the server from R2 and treat that reply as proof of the client return path.
Capture the client gateway ARP exchange again before examining reply forwarding.
explanation: The server received the request, so check the server's route and neighbor entry for the reply to the client.

whyWrong.0: R2 already has a return route, and the server's next hop is the open question.
whyWrong.2: A ping to R2 uses a different destination than the client reply.
whyWrong.3: The request arrived, so the client gateway's ARP is not the issue.

exhibit.title: Matched observations for one attempt
exhibit.text:
Client 10.31.10.50 sends to server 10.31.20.10.
Server capture sees that request. Client capture sees no reply.
Server is /24; its route/default-gateway configuration has not been inspected.
R2 route to 10.31.10.0/24 is present.

prompt: A service test works from the router source but fails for the client. What should you check next?
options: Capture only R1-originated replies and use them to clear the client access path.
Repeat the router-source service test until five successive attempts pass.
Compare client-source policy and the client-facing ingress path.
Increase the client's retry timeout before comparing how its flow is handled.
explanation: The router test uses a different source address and skips the client-facing ingress path. Compare the policy and ingress path that the client's traffic uses.

whyWrong.0: Router-originated replies say nothing about the client's source or ingress.
whyWrong.1: Repeating the router test still avoids the client path.
whyWrong.3: A timer change does not address the source and path difference.

exhibit.title: Different-origin test paths
exhibit.text:
PC-A reaches its gateway but cannot reach a remote service.
R1 reaches that service with source set to its LAN interface address.
PC-A's address, mask and gateway match the plan.
Client-source policy and ingress handling have not been checked.

prompt: What are the IOS ping defaults?
options: Five 100-byte packets with a two-second timeout
Four 32-byte packets with a four-second timeout
Five 1500-byte packets with a one-second timeout
Ten 64-byte packets with a two-second timeout
explanation: IOS ping sends five 100-byte ICMP echo packets and waits two seconds for each reply.

whyWrong.1: Four 32-byte packets is the Windows default.
whyWrong.2: IOS defaults to 100-byte packets and a two-second timeout.
whyWrong.3: IOS sends five packets by default.

prompt: What happens to a link when the two ends are set to different fixed speeds?
options: The link stays down
The link comes up with late collisions
The link comes up and runs at the lower speed
The link comes up with CRC errors only
explanation: A speed mismatch leaves the link down. A duplex mismatch brings the link up with late collisions on the half-duplex end.

whyWrong.1: Late collisions are the sign of a duplex mismatch, not a speed mismatch.
whyWrong.2: Mismatched fixed speeds do not negotiate down to the lower speed.
whyWrong.3: CRC errors on the full-duplex end belong to a duplex mismatch.

prompt: An interface was shut down with the `shutdown` command. Which status pair does it show?
options: administratively down/down
down/down (no carrier)
up/down (protocol down)
up/up (working link)
explanation: A locally shut interface shows administratively down/down. Down/down means no carrier, and up/down means a Layer 2 problem.

whyWrong.1: Down/down means the physical layer is down, not that the interface was shut down by command.
whyWrong.2: Up/down means the physical link is up but the line protocol is down.
whyWrong.3: Up/up is a working interface.

prompt: Which syslog severity is level 0?
options: Emergencies
Alerts
Critical
Debugging
explanation: Severity 0 is emergencies, the most severe. Severity 7 is debugging.

whyWrong.1: Alerts is severity 1.
whyWrong.2: Critical is severity 2.
whyWrong.3: Debugging is severity 7.
